name: Stencil AI
what: An app that turns a photo, sketch or design into a print-ready tattoo stencil for tattoo artists.
title: Stencil AI went from $16K to $63K a month in 2026 by fixing one boring job for tattoo artists
dek: Two brothers, one of them a tattoo artist, built a tool that skips hours of hand-tracing. They charged from day one, sold on the web first, then put it on the App Store.
pattern: Start with a problem someone close to you has

numbers.k: MRR (money coming in each month from subscriptions)
numbers.label: Verified

first_revenue.text: Already $16,032 in January 2026, the first month TrustMRR shows, before the iPhone app came out.
first_revenue.label: Verified

first_customers.text: Not public. The website was selling paid plans to tattoo artists before the app launched, and in Feb 2026 an Instagram bio link pointed to it.
first_customers.label: Wayback

team.text: TrustMRR lists 1 founder. The company's own site lists two co-founder brothers (a programmer and a tattoo artist) plus a senior artist advisor.
team.label: Sources differ

phases.name: A problem in the family
phases.story: Before every tattoo, artists trace the design by hand into a clean line drawing called a stencil, then transfer it onto skin. The team behind Stencil AI is two brothers. One is the programmer, the other is a tattoo artist, so the problem was sitting right next to the person who could code a fix.
phases.lesson: The best problems to solve are ones a friend or family member deals with every week.

phases.name: Web first, paid from the start
phases.story: The website was already online by September 2025. In February 2026 the homepage promised "a perfect stencil in 30 seconds" and there was no free plan: $14, $29 or $69 a month. The phone app was still marked "Coming soon". In January 2026 it already brought in about $16,000.
phases.lesson: You don't need an app store listing to start charging. A simple website with a price tests whether people will pay.

phases.name: Selling to professionals
phases.story: Stencil AI is sold to people who earn money with it. A Studio plan charges per artist, so a whole tattoo shop can pay for it. The pitch is time: the October 2026 homepage says it "replaces hours of tracing in Procreate", a drawing app.
phases.lesson: People pay more easily for a tool that saves them time at work than for one that is just fun.

phases.name: The App Store launch
phases.story: The iPhone app went live on March 12, 2026, with an Android version too. Monthly revenue grew every month from January to July, from about $16,000 to about $62,000.
phases.lesson: Once the website proves people pay, an app puts the tool where the customer works: on a phone or tablet at the chair.

phases.name: Holding steady and getting found
phases.story: Since July, revenue has stayed between about $60,000 and $64,000 a month. The site has a blog of how-to guides, like how to print a stencil or make one in Procreate, so artists searching Google land on it. Its MRR was $48,693 when we read it, lower than October's $62,976. Both numbers are real but measure different things: MRR only counts subscriptions active on the day it was read, as a monthly amount, while a month's revenue is all the money collected that month, which can include yearly plans paid up front. The TrustMRR listing names app store search, SEO (getting found on Google), a blog, TikTok, Instagram, Pinterest and YouTube as its channels.
phases.lesson: Write the guide your customer is already searching for, and put your tool inside it.

wayback.headline: Turn any photo into a perfect stencil in 30 seconds
wayback.sub: Better stencils mean better tattoos and happier clients.
wayback.prices: Hobby $14/mo, Pro $29/mo, Studio $69/mo (2 artists, +$25 per extra artist)

wayback.headline: Turn any photo into a perfect stencil in 30 seconds
wayback.sub: The tattoo stencil maker that replaces hours of tracing in Procreate.

checklist: Ask three people you know what boring task they repeat every week at work. Write the answers down.
Pick one job with a clear before and after (a photo before, a stencil after) and sketch what a tool would do.
Make a one-page website that shows the result and a price before you build a full app.
Ask one person who does the job for real to test your output and tell you what is wrong with it.
Write one how-to guide that answers a question your customers type into Google.
Put your link in your Instagram or TikTok bio and count the clicks for a week.
